\begin{document}

\title{Don't Reweight, Calibrate: Per-Label Class Weights Distort Top-$K$ Ranking, the Textbook Inversion Does Not Repair It, and Per-Label Calibration Does}

\author{Akifumi Goto}
\email{souldrive7@gmail.com}
\affiliation{\institution{Independent researcher}\country{Japan}}

\begin{abstract}
Systems that rank $L$ labels per row (a customer's next product, a document's tags) routinely train one-vs-rest models with a label-specific positive-class weight such as \texttt{scale\_pos\_weight}$=n_-/n_+$ to counter imbalance. The textbook account of the consequence is Elkan's identity: a weight $w_j$ shifts label $j$'s log-odds by $\ln w_j$, so the model ranks by $w_j\cdot\mathrm{odds}(p_{ij})$ instead of the marginal $p_{ij}$ that is Bayes-optimal for precision@$K$, and the shift can be undone analytically. Whether that account describes what a finite learner does with weights in the thousands or millions, and which post-hoc repair then works, has not been measured. On the Santander product-recommendation benchmark (\nnTest{} test rows, \nnLabels{} labels) we decompose the top-$K$ loss of a weighted LightGBM ranker with a what-if device, an analytic inversion, and a ladder of post-hoc repairs. The ideal odds shift explains only a fifth of the loss; the rest is a per-label monotone distortion produced by leaf saturation, which the inversion cannot undo but per-label calibration can, provided that labels without calibration positives are mapped to their prior: $\mapseven$ goes from $\nNraw$ (unweighted) to $\nSraw$ (weighted) and back to $\nSplIsoPrior$ after per-label isotonic regression, while the identity fallback collapses a direct-probability model instead. Dose-response experiments on \nnMulan{} MULAN benchmarks with \nnLearners{} learners and a synthetic study with known marginals reproduce the odds shift, its exact inversion under a realizable learner, the failure of the inversion under capacity limits, and the harm of per-label calibration when calibration positives are scarce. The recommendation is to estimate marginals with an unweighted proper loss, calibrate per label with a prior fallback, and decide at top-$K$.
\end{abstract}

\maketitle

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Ranking many binary labels within a row is the operational core of product recommendation, tagging, and risk triage: for each customer the system scores every product, sorts, and shows the top $K$~\cite{Jain2016XMLLoss,Menon2019Reductions}. The labels are almost always imbalanced, and the most common remedy in gradient-boosting practice is a per-label positive-class weight, \texttt{scale\_pos\_weight} in XGBoost and LightGBM~\cite{Chen2016XGBoost,Ke2017LightGBM}, for which the XGBoost documentation suggests $n_-/n_+$~\cite{XGBoostDocs}; the same recipe is \texttt{pos\_weight} in binary cross-entropy for neural multi-label models.

Label-specific weights are not a free choice when the deliverable is a per-row ranking. Two facts are classical. Ranking labels by their marginal $p_{ij}=\Pr(y_{ij}=1\mid x_i)$ is Bayes-optimal for precision@$K$, and one-vs-rest training with a proper loss is consistent for it~\cite{Dembczynski2012Univariate,Menon2019Reductions,Wydmuch2018PLT}. A positive-class weight $w$ moves the population minimizer of a proper loss from $p$ to $wp/(wp+1-p)$, an odds shift by $w$~\cite{Elkan2001,Saerens2002}. Together they say that a label-specific $w_j$ makes the model rank by $w_j\cdot\mathrm{odds}(p_{ij})$, a different ranking whenever the weights differ, and the XGBoost documentation itself warns that a re-balanced model no longer predicts the right probability~\cite{XGBoostDocs}.

What the classical account leaves open is what a finite-capacity learner does when $w_j$ is in the thousands or millions, as the recommended value is for rare labels, and which post-hoc repair then works. Per-label isotonic regression is known to break top-$k$ accuracy in multi-class settings~\cite{Patel2021IMax}, and the extreme multi-label literature deliberately uses one shared monotone map so that precision@$k$ is untouched, deferring per-label calibration to future work~\cite{Ullah2025XMLCCalib}. Neither line measures the cross-label consequence of training weights, nor the role of the calibrator's behaviour on labels that have no calibration positives.

\Cref{fig:one} gives our answer on the Santander benchmark. Applying the ideal odds shift to an unweighted LightGBM predicts a fraction of the loss that the trained weighted model actually suffers; the remainder is a per-label monotone distortion that we trace to leaf saturation (\cref{lem:leaf}), that the analytic inversion cannot undo, and that per-label calibration repairs up to a small residue above the in-sample ceiling. The repair works only if a single implementation detail is right: a label without calibration positives must be mapped to its prior, not passed through, otherwise the untouched labels occupy the top of every row (\cref{prop:dead}).

\paragraph{Contributions}
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,nosep]
\item \textbf{Where the textbook account stops.} Using Elkan's identity as a what-if device we separate the top-$K$ loss of a weighted ranker into the ideal odds shift, a further per-label monotone distortion, and a residue above the in-sample per-label ceiling (\cref{fig:one}A, \cref{tab:ladder}). On Santander the shift is the minor part; the leaf-level condition behind the rest (\cref{lem:leaf}) is confirmed exactly on single trees.
\item \textbf{The fallback decides the sign.} Per-label isotonic regression improves all three Santander base models when labels without calibration positives are mapped to their prior, and collapses a direct-probability model when they keep their raw scores (\cref{prop:dead}, \cref{fig:one}B); a shared map never inverts a pair and therefore repairs nothing beyond tie resolution (\cref{rem:shared}). On Santander every calibrated label has hundreds of calibration positives.
\item \textbf{Dose-response and a recipe.} Across \nnMulan{} MULAN benchmarks, \nnLearners{} learners and a synthetic study with known marginals, the odds shift is learner-agnostic and exactly invertible for a realizable learner, the inversion fails once the learner saturates, and per-label calibration hurts where labels have few calibration positives (\cref{tab:mulan}, \cref{app:mulan,app:synthetic}). The recipe is: unweighted proper loss, per-label calibration with a prior fallback chosen on the calibration split, decision at top-$K$.
\end{enumerate}
All numbers are generated by one script from result files that will be released with the paper; the dead-label policy of every calibrator is explicit.

\section{Setup and Theory}
\label{sec:theory}

Rows $i=1,\dots,n$ carry features $x_i$ and binary labels $y_{ij}$, $j=1,\dots,L$; $p_{ij}=\Pr(y_{ij}=1\mid x_i)$ is the marginal and $\pi_j=\Pr(y_{ij}=1)$ the prevalence. A scorer returns $s_{ij}$ and the system shows the $K$ largest scores of row $i$. We evaluate with $\mapk$ in the Kaggle definition (average precision at $K$ per row, averaged over rows with at least one positive) and report per-row bootstrap intervals. For precision@$K$ the population-optimal ranking sorts by $p_{ij}$, and one-vs-rest with a proper loss is consistent for it~\cite{Dembczynski2012Univariate,Koyejo2015Consistent,Menon2019Reductions}. A post-hoc calibrator is \emph{separable} if it maps label $j$ by a non-decreasing $g_j$ independently of the other labels; per-label Platt, isotonic, temperature and beta calibration are separable, and so is the shared (pooled) isotonic map of~\cite{Ullah2025XMLCCalib} with $g_j\equiv g$. A positive-class weight $w_j>0$ multiplies the loss of the positives of label $j$ (\texttt{scale\_pos\_weight}, \texttt{pos\_weight}).

\begin{remark}[Shared maps never invert, distinct maps can]
\label{rem:shared}
If $g_1=\dots=g_L$ the calibrator never creates a strict inversion within a row, so a shared map is rank-neutral up to ties and can repair nothing beyond tie resolution. If two continuous maps differ at an interior point, some row's strict order is inverted. Both halves are folklore (\cref{app:proof}); shared class-wise binning~\cite{Patel2021IMax}, intra-order-preserving maps~\cite{Rahimi2020IntraOrder} and the shared map of~\cite{Ullah2025XMLCCalib} rely on the first. A per-label map can reorder, and in the population limit it should: calibrated per-label maps return the marginals. Per-label calibration therefore hurts only through estimation error, whose boundary case is a label without calibration positives (\cref{prop:dead}).
\end{remark}

\begin{proposition}[Odds shift, after Elkan]
\label{prop:odds}
Let $q_{ij}$ be the population minimizer of a strictly proper binary loss with positive-class weight $w_j$. Then $\operatorname{logit}q_{ij}=\operatorname{logit}p_{ij}+\ln w_j$~\cite{Elkan2001,Saerens2002}, and for $p_{ij}>p_{ik}$ the weighted scores reverse the pair iff $\operatorname{logit}p_{ij}-\operatorname{logit}p_{ik}<\ln w_k-\ln w_j$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The weighted loss is the unweighted loss under the tilted distribution whose posterior odds are $w_j$ times the original; the flip condition is the difference of the shifted logits.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
\label{cor:odds}
(a) A common weight $w_j\equiv w$ is a shared map and never changes within-row order. (b) The flipped pairs, hence the top-$K$ loss of the \emph{ideal} weighted model, depend only on the unweighted logit gaps and the intended weights, so they can be computed from an unweighted model before weighted training (\emph{what-if}); this describes a learner that realizes the shift exactly, not necessarily the one a finite learner produces. (c) When $w_jp_{ij}\ll1$, $q_{ij}\approx w_jp_{ij}$, so weighted training approximates the optimal ranking for a propensity-weighted precision@$K$ with propensities $1/w_j$~\cite{Jain2016XMLLoss,Wydmuch2021PSPLT}: training weights silently change the metric. If a utility-weighted ranking is wanted, multiplying calibrated marginals by the utilities is exact.
\end{corollary}

\begin{lemma}[Leaf saturation]
\label{lem:leaf}
For weighted log-loss the optimal constant in a tree leaf with $n_+$ positives and $n_-$ negatives is $\rho(w)=wn_+/(wn_++n_-)$. Any leaf with $n_+\ge1$ satisfies $\rho(w)\ge1-n_-/(wn_+)$, so its prediction is within $\varepsilon$ of one once $w\ge n_-/(\varepsilon n_+)$; all test cells routed to such leaves tie near one and lose their order across those leaves.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
$-wn_+\ln\rho-n_-\ln(1-\rho)$ is minimized at $\rho=wn_+/(wn_++n_-)$, and $1-\rho=n_-/(wn_++n_-)\le n_-/(wn_+)$.
\end{proof}

The lemma is exact for a single tree whose leaf values are weighted class frequencies and describes the fixed point that a boosted ensemble approaches when it fits the weighted objective well; it is the tree analogue of importance weights losing their effect on a flexible learner~\cite{Byrd2019}. With the recommended $w_j\approx1/\pi_j$ and leaves of at most $m$ negatives, every positive-containing leaf of a label with $\pi_j\le\varepsilon/m$ is within $\varepsilon$ of one. Two consequences follow and should be kept apart. The realized shift is no longer the constant $\ln w_j$ of \cref{prop:odds}, so the analytic inversion $q\mapsto q/(q+w(1-q))$ stops working, but the distortion is still monotone within each label, so a per-label monotone map fitted on calibration data can undo it. And the cells tied at one within a label have lost their mutual order, which no separable map recovers; this part is bounded by the gap between the in-sample per-label ceiling and the unweighted model.

\begin{proposition}[Identity fallback occupies the top]
\label{prop:dead}
Let label $d$ have no calibration positives and keep its raw score $s_{id}$, while every calibrated label $j$ is mapped by $g_j$ with $g_j(s)\le\bar q$ for all $s$ (isotonic outputs are bounded by the largest block mean of the calibration split). If $s_{id}>\bar q$ then $d$ is ranked above every calibrated label in row $i$ regardless of $y_{id}$; with $m$ such labels, $m$ of the top-$K$ slots are occupied by them.
\end{proposition}
The condition holds whenever raw scores are inflated relative to calibrated ones, which is the situation that motivates calibration. scikit-learn's \texttt{IsotonicRegression} returns the constant zero on a single-class split and \texttt{LogisticRegression} raises; our own earlier one-vs-rest code, and any loop that catches the failure and passes the score through, returns the input unchanged. A prior fallback ($\tilde s_{id}=\hat\pi_d$) or exclusion removes the effect.

\paragraph{Data and models.} The Santander Product Recommendation data~\cite{KaggleSantander2016} has \nnLabels{} products; we use the public time split with \nnTrain{} training rows and \nnTest{} test rows and the Kaggle $\mapseven$. Three base scorers produce test probabilities for every cell: \Nm, LightGBM one-vs-rest without weights (100 trees, learning rate $0.05$, 31 leaves); \Sm, LightGBM one-vs-rest with the same learning rate and leaf count but 60 trees and $w_j=n_{-,j}/n_{+,j}$ per label (between \nwMin{} and \nwMax); and \Wm, a Wasserstein gradient-boosting model with Beta outputs~\cite{Matsubara2024WGBoost} that estimates probabilities directly without weights. Both LightGBM runs share the feature pipeline and the time split. Calibrators are fitted on a random 30\% of the test rows (seed 42, \nnVal{} rows) and evaluated on the remaining 70\%; \nSnDead{} labels have no positives in the calibration split, and every calibrated label has hundreds. Bootstrap intervals use $B=\nbootB$ per-row resamples of the \nbootN{} evaluation rows with a positive.

\paragraph{Decomposition and repair ladder (\cref{fig:one}, \cref{tab:ladder}).} The weighted model loses $\nSloss$ $\mapseven$ against \Nm; we express every repair as the share of this loss it returns. Adding $\ln w_j$ to the logits of \Nm is the ideal weighted model of \cref{prop:odds}; it scores $\nwhatifIdeal$, changes the top-7 set of \nfracRowsChangedWhatif\% of the first $500{,}000$ rows while keeping \noverlapWhatif{} of 7 items, and accounts for \noddsShare\% of the loss. The trained \Sm keeps only \noverlapS{} of 7 items, has \nSsatOne\% of its cells at exactly $1.0$ and \nSsatZero\% at exactly $0.0$, and the analytic inversion with the known $w_j$ returns \nelkanShare\% ($\nSelkan$). The remaining distortion is that of \cref{lem:leaf}, and the ladder measures its shape by what each repair reaches. An intercept-only logit shift fitted per label on the calibration split returns \noffsetShare\% ($\nSplOffsetPrior$), so for most labels the realized shift is a constant that differs from $\ln w_j$; per-label Platt scaling returns \nplattShare\% and beta calibration \nbetaShare\%; per-label isotonic regression with the prior fallback returns \nrepairShare\% ($\nSplIsoPrior$, i.e.\ \nrepairExtraShare\% beyond the odds shift), within $\nSplIsoPriorCeilGap$ of the in-sample per-label ceiling ($\nSceil$); the remaining \ntieShare\% ($\nSceilGap$) lies above that ceiling, and the cells tied at exactly $1.0$ or $0.0$ are its visible cause. The bootstrap difference between \Nm raw and the repaired \Sm is $\nciNminusS$. Two symptoms agree: the mean within-label AUC (200{,}000-row subsample), which no monotone map can change, drops from $\nNauc$ (\Nm) to $\nSauc$ (\Sm), and the ceiling of \Sm stays below the raw $\nNraw$ of \Nm. Pooled isotonic leaves \Wm and \Nm unchanged, as \cref{rem:shared} requires, and moves \Sm from $\nSraw$ to $\nSpooled$ only because pooled blocks merge the tied cells and the stable sort breaks ties by label index; no strictly ordered pair is inverted. A label-free per-label shift chosen so that the mean prediction matches training prevalence~\cite{Saerens2002} reaches $\nSlabelFree$ (\nlabelFreeShare\%) without labels, but for \nnCappedShift{} of the \nnLabels{} labels the target is unreachable because more cells are exactly $1.0$ than the prevalence allows; we report it as evidence that a per-label constant recovers most of the loss, not as a repair to deploy.

\paragraph{The fallback decides the sign.} With the identity fallback, per-label isotonic regression yields $\nSplIsoId$ on \Sm (\nSplIsoIdRel\% relative to raw, below the popularity baseline: $\nciSidMinusPop$ against $\npopMAP$) and collapses \Wm from $\nWraw$ to $\nWplIsoId$ (\nWplIsoIdRel\%): the \nSnDead{} dead labels keep their raw scores (mean $\nWdeadRawMean$ on \Wm) while every calibrated label shrinks to its prevalence (largest mean $\nWaliveCalMax$), so all three sit in the top 7 of \nWdeadAllRowsPct\% of rows, exactly as \cref{prop:dead} says. This is where the well-known claim that per-label calibration hurts top-$K$ belongs. With the prior fallback the same calibrator gives $\nSplIsoPrior$ on \Sm, $\nWplIsoPrior$ on \Wm (\nWplIsoPriorRel\%, $\nciWprior$) and $\nNplIsoPrior$ on \Nm (\nNplIsoPriorRel\%, $\nciNprior$), each within $0.01$ of its ceiling ($\nSceil$, $\nWceil$, $\nNceil$); exclusion behaves like the prior. The three dead labels also have no positives in the evaluation split, so the prior costs nothing here; on data where a label is rare in the calibration split but alive at test time, the prior trades that label's recall for the others' precision. Per-label Platt and beta calibration repair \Sm almost as well and come within $\nNplPlattIsoGap$ and $\nNplBetaIsoGap$ of isotonic on \Nm, but leave \Wm at its raw level ($\nWplPlattPrior$) and the intercept-only shift lowers it to $\nWplOffsetPrior$: the gain on \Wm comes from label-specific non-linear maps that one- and two-parameter families cannot express.

\paragraph{MULAN benchmarks.} We retrain one-vs-rest models on \nnMulan{} MULAN datasets~\cite{Tsoumakas2011MULAN} with $w_j\in\{1,\sqrt{r_j},r_j,10r_j\}$, $r_j=n_{-,j}/n_{+,j}$, and \nnLearners{} learners: LightGBM in a default and a strongly regularized configuration, XGBoost, $\ell_2$-regularized logistic regression with sample weights, and a two-layer MLP with per-label \texttt{pos\_weight}. \Cref{tab:mulan} shows the default LightGBM cells and \cref{app:mulan} every cell. Three regularities hold. (i) For the tree learners raw $\mapk$ falls with the weight magnitude on genbase and enron and, under regularization, on medical, whereas logistic regression and XGBoost on medical gain from weights ($\nmedLogregRawWone\to\nmedLogregRawWr$ and $\nmedXgbRawWone\to\nmedXgbRawWr$ at $w{=}r$); on the \nnMulanModest{} datasets with $\max r<100$ the change at $w{=}r$ is at most $\nmaxDropModest$ and of either sign, in line with the ``class weights are benign'' reports at imbalance ratios below 70~\cite{Liu2026Resampling}. (ii) The what-if prediction is within $0.03$ of the trained weighted model on \nnWhatifClose{} of \nnMulan{} datasets; it under-predicts the loss where the trained model saturates (genbase: $\ngenbaseDefaultWhatifWr$ predicted, $\ngenbaseDefaultRawWr$ trained, distinct scores per label \ngenbaseDistinctWone{} to \ngenbaseDistinctWr) and over-predicts it where regularization shrinks the realized shift (enron, strongly regularized: $\nenronStrongWhatifWr$ against $\nenronStrongRawWr$), and where no saturation occurs the analytic inversion recovers the unweighted ranking (enron, strongly regularized: $\nenronStrongRawWone$ at $w{=}1$, $\nenronStrongRawWr$ at $w{=}r$, $\nenronStrongInvWr$ after inversion). (iii) Where the number of distinct scores per label collapses, the ceiling falls and neither inversion nor calibration returns to the unweighted level (medical, strongly regularized: $\nmedStrongDistinctWone$ to $\nmedStrongDistinctWtenr$ distinct scores and ceiling $\nmedStrongCeilWone$ to $\nmedStrongCeilWtenr$ from $w{=}1$ to $10r$); on medical, where \nmedDeadCal{} of \nmedL{} labels have no calibration positives, the identity fallback loses to the prior by up to $\nmedIdVsPriorMaxGap$. The sweep also contains the negative result the recipe must carry: with few calibration positives, per-label isotonic regression with the prior fallback \emph{hurts} an unweighted model. With the default LightGBM at $w{=}1$ it lowers $\mapk$ by more than $0.005$ on \nnHurtDefault{} of \nnMulan{} datasets (birds $\nbirdsRawWone\to\nbirdsPlIsoPriorWone$ with a median of \ncalPosMedBirds{} calibration positives per label, medical $\nmedRawWone\to\nmedPlIsoPriorWone$ with \ncalPosMedMedical) and changes it by at most $\nmaxAbsDeltaElsewhere$ elsewhere; across learners the sign varies from dataset to dataset. The median number of calibration positives does not separate the cases cleanly (genbase and enron gain slightly with \ncalPosMedGenbase{} and \ncalPosMedEnron, flags loses with \ncalPosMedFlags), so the threshold below which a label keeps the prior must be chosen on the calibration split rather than fixed in advance.

\paragraph{Leaf saturation.} Single decision trees with \texttt{class\_weight}$=\{1{:}w\}$ have leaf values equal to the weighted class frequencies, so the saturation share computed from each leaf's $(n_+,n_-)$ and $w$ equals the measured share of predictions within $10^{-3}$ of one; \cref{app:leaf} reports this exact check and the LightGBM sweep across \texttt{min\_child\_samples} and $w\in\{1,r,10r,100r\}$. On these small datasets the saturated share stays below \nleafLgbmMaxSat\% and the ceiling moves only where the number of distinct scores collapses (medical, \texttt{min\_child\_samples}$=50$: ceiling $\nleafMedCeilFiftyWone$ at $w{=}1$, $\nleafMedCeilFiftyWhundred$ at $100r$). The Santander weights ($w_j$ up to \nwMax) lie far beyond this sweep, which is where the ceiling falls below the unweighted raw score.

\paragraph{Synthetic study.} With known marginals (\cref{app:synthetic}) a realizable learner (logistic regression) attains the Bayes optimum unweighted ($\nsynLRrawDeZero$ against $\nsynTrueD$), weights degrade the ranking monotonically in the spread of $\ln w_j$, and the analytic inversion restores the optimum exactly ($\nsynLRinvD$): \cref{prop:odds} is the whole story. A deliberately small LightGBM fails to invert ($\nsynSmallInvD$) although its in-sample ceiling is intact ($\nsynSmallCeilD$), while XGBoost and the MLP, with more capacity, still invert. The study reproduces the odds shift, its exact inversion and the failure of the inversion under capacity limits; it does not reproduce a ceiling loss of the Santander size, because even where a quarter of the cells saturate the ceiling moves by about $0.01$.

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Consistency and top-$K$.} One-vs-rest surrogates are consistent for the rank loss~\cite{Dembczynski2012Univariate} and, with a proper loss, for precision@$k$~\cite{Menon2019Reductions}; multi-label metrics decompose into per-label decisions on the marginals~\cite{Koyejo2015Consistent}, and the precision@$k$ regret of a plug-in ranker is bounded by its marginal error~\cite{Wydmuch2018PLT}. Propensity-scored metrics weight labels deliberately~\cite{Jain2016XMLLoss,Wydmuch2021PSPLT,Schultheis2023GTU}; \cref{cor:odds}(c) shows that training weights approximate that ranking implicitly. An instance-level weight is constant within a row and rank-neutral; a label-level weight is not.

\paragraph{Imbalance corrections and calibration.} Elkan's identity~\cite{Elkan2001} and the prior-shift correction of~\cite{Saerens2002} give the odds-shift map, which logit adjustment applies post hoc in long-tailed learning~\cite{Menon2021LogitAdjust}. Probability estimates under imbalance corrections are unreliable~\cite{Wallace2012}, undersampling is corrected by an odds shift~\cite{DalPozzolo2015}, class-weighted models can be inverted analytically~\cite{Caplin2022ClassWeights}, and imbalance corrections harm calibration in clinical models without improving discrimination~\cite{VandenGoorbergh2022}; a recent tree-ensemble study at imbalance ratios up to 70 finds class weights benign for calibration error and Platt or isotonic recalibration sufficient~\cite{Liu2026Resampling}, which our modest-imbalance MULAN results confirm, and importance weights are known to lose their effect on learners that can fit the weighted objective~\cite{Byrd2019}. The XGBoost documentation recommends $n_-/n_+$ and warns about probabilities~\cite{XGBoostDocs}; class-balanced losses for GBDT and long-tailed multi-label vision~\cite{Luo2024GBDTImb,Wu2020DBLoss}, classical post-hoc calibration~\cite{Zadrozny2002,NiculescuMizil2005,Guo2017Calibration}, and calibrator selection and benchmarks~\cite{Abdelrahman2025SmartCal,Berta2026CalArena} optimize calibration error, not ranking. None measures the cross-label consequence of label-specific weights or the saturation regime.

\paragraph{Calibration versus ranking.} Shared class-wise calibration recovers the top-5 accuracy lost by independent per-class maps on ImageNet~\cite{Patel2021IMax}; intra-order-preserving maps, Mix-n-Match and Meta-Cal are rank-preserving multi-class calibrators~\cite{Rahimi2020IntraOrder,Zhang2020MixNMatch,Ma2021MetaCal}, Dirichlet calibration is not~\cite{Kull2019Dirichlet}, and the rate at which calibrators change the top-1 prediction has been quantified~\cite{Kim2026Confidence}. In multi-label and extreme classification a shared monotone map keeps precision@$k$ untouched and per-label calibration is deferred to future work~\cite{Ullah2025XMLCCalib}; label-wise monotone maps serve reliability reranking~\cite{Tae2026Reranking}, group-wise calibrators shrunk toward a global map are analysed in~\cite{Lavi2025Clustered}, per-class residual offsets are Bayes-optimal for reranking when the distortion is class-separable~\cite{Wang2026BeyondLA}, and normalization-aware, tag-marginal and utility-aware calibration address neighbouring settings~\cite{Arad2025NAIso,Kranzlein2021Marginal,Hegazy2025Utility}. Recommender systems calibrate per rank group, learn monotone layers that keep a ranker's order, correct sampling bias by an additive logit term, and face maximization bias when selected items are evaluated~\cite{Sato2024TopN,Bai2025UnconstrainedMono,Cheng2026IsotonicLayer,Yi2019SamplingBias,Fan2023CalibMatters}; calibration of a distribution over rankings is formalized in~\cite{Thies2026CalibLR}, top-$K$ ranking measures are related in~\cite{Wang2024TKPR}, and ``calibrated label ranking''~\cite{Furnkranz2008CLR} is unrelated to probability calibration. Relative to this line our contribution is the source of the label-wise distortion (training weights), the what-if bound on its odds-shift part, its saturation regime, and the role of the dead-label fallback.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Recipe.} Estimate marginals with an unweighted proper loss; if imbalance makes optimization hard, prefer a common weight (rank-neutral by \cref{cor:odds}(a)) or regularization over label-specific weights. Calibrate per label on a held-out split, map every label whose calibration positives cannot support its map to the prior rather than the identity, and choose that positives threshold, and the choice between per-label and shared maps, on the calibration split. A shared map is rank-neutral up to ties and is the safe choice when the split is small. If a utility- or propensity-weighted ranking is wanted, multiply calibrated marginals by the utilities at decision time. Without labels, the share of cells at exactly $1.0$ and the number of distinct scores per label flag saturation and predict that the analytic inversion will fail, though not how much top-$K$ is lost.

\paragraph{Limitations.} The large-scale evidence is one benchmark with 24 labels; the MULAN datasets are small. The two Santander LightGBM runs differ in the number of boosting rounds (100 versus 60), so the decomposition compares models that are not identical in capacity; the MULAN and synthetic sweeps, where every weighted model has exactly the configuration of its unweighted counterpart, show the same two mechanisms. Boosted trees are the main learner family; the saturation lemma is stated for trees, and the logistic-regression and MLP results show only that the odds shift is learner-agnostic. The oracle ceiling is an empirical reference, not a bound on all post-hoc procedures, and row-dependent calibrators~\cite{Rahimi2020IntraOrder} are outside the separable class. Per-label calibration needs calibration positives and hurts on birds and medical for every learner; no threshold in the median number of calibration positives separates the harmful from the harmless cases in our sweep. The Santander calibrators are fitted on rows of the test period and therefore also absorb the prior shift between training and test months that the popularity baseline does not see. The label-free prevalence-matching shift is infeasible for \nnCappedShift{} of \nnLabels{} labels and is not proposed as a repair. Saturation depends on how far a leaf may move per round: LightGBM's \texttt{max\_delta\_step} is unbounded by default, whereas the XGBoost tuning page recommends a finite value for imbalanced logistic loss~\cite{XGBoostDocs}; we did not sweep it, and a cap would lower the share of cells at exactly $1.0$ and may let the inversion recover more.

\paragraph{Conclusion.} Per-label class weights change the target of one-vs-rest training from the marginal to a weighted odds, and on a large recommendation benchmark the textbook odds shift is the minor part of the resulting top-$K$ loss; the major part is a per-label monotone distortion produced by saturation, which the analytic inversion cannot undo. Per-label calibration with a prior fallback undoes it up to the small residue above the in-sample ceiling, and the fallback, not the calibrator, decides the sign. Reweighting is the wrong tool for a per-row ranking; unweighted estimation followed by per-label calibration with the right fallback is the right one.

\section*{Reproducibility}
All scores, calibrators and tables are produced by the \texttt{code/} directory of the repository that will be released with this paper, from two fixed prediction arrays (SHA-256 recorded in the result files) and the public MULAN ARFF files (content hashes recorded). The two Santander LightGBM runs share the feature pipeline and the time split; the unweighted run's configuration is recorded in its metadata and the weighted run's tree count is the default of its training script. The synthetic generator, the leaf-saturation check and the bootstrap use fixed seeds, and the dead-label policy is a named argument of every calibrator.

\section{Shared and distinct separable maps}
\label{app:proof}
\begin{proposition}
\label{prop:sep}
Let $g_1,\dots,g_L$ be non-decreasing maps on a common interval $I$. (a) If $g_1=\dots=g_L$, the separable calibrator never creates a strict inversion: $s_{ij}>s_{ik}$ implies $\tilde s_{ij}\ge\tilde s_{ik}$, with equality only when both scores fall in the same plateau of the shared map. (b) If the maps are continuous and $g_j(a)\neq g_k(a)$ for some interior $a\in I$ and some $j\neq k$, there is a score vector whose strict within-row order is inverted.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
(a) is monotonicity. (b) Say $g_j(a)<g_k(a)$. By continuity of $g_j$ there is $b>a$ in $I$ with $g_j(b)<g_k(a)$; the row with $s_{ij}=b>a=s_{ik}$ has $\tilde s_{ij}<\tilde s_{ik}$. If no such $b$ exists because $a$ is the right endpoint, use continuity of $g_k$ to pick $b<a$ with $g_k(b)>g_j(a)$ and the row $s_{ik}=b<a=s_{ij}$.
\end{proof}
